spring-wire-by-type.title: Wire a bean graph by type
spring-wire-by-type.description:
A Spring container keeps a list of **bean definitions**. When a bean's constructor asks for a parameter of some
type, the container looks for the bean that **is of that type** (its own class or any interface it implements) and
passes it in. Build that lookup.

`wire(beans)` receives a list of dicts:

- `name` — the bean name,
- `types` — every type the bean can be seen as (its class first, then its interfaces),
- `needs` — the types of its constructor parameters, in order.

Return a dict that maps every bean name to the list of **bean names** injected into it, in parameter order.
If a needed type matches no bean, return the string `"NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: <type>"` for the first
problem found (scan beans in list order, parameters left to right). The input guarantees that a type never
matches more than one bean.

**Example:** a bean `orderService` needing `["BookRepository"]` and a bean `jdbcBookRepository` whose types are
`["JdbcBookRepository", "BookRepository"]` → `{"orderService": ["jdbcBookRepository"], "jdbcBookRepository": []}`.

guide.prereqs: Python lists and dicts. The lesson *The application context and @Bean* explains what a bean is.
guide.intuition: Injection by type is a search: for each constructor parameter, find the one bean that can be viewed as that type. An interface counts, which is why `types` holds more than the class name.
hints: Handle one bean at a time, and inside it one needed type at a time.
A bean matches when the needed type appears anywhere in its `types` list, not only at index 0.
Return the error string immediately when a search comes back empty; otherwise collect the names.
guide.brute_force: The direct double loop (for every need, scan all beans) is already what is asked. It costs O(B · N · T) for B beans, N needs and T types per bean.
guide.complexity: Time O(B · N · T) with the scan, O(total types + total needs) with an index. Space O(B + N).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing only against the class name misses interface injection, the most common style. Silently skipping a missing type hides the error Spring would raise at start-up.
guide.follow_up: What should happen when two beans match? That is the next problem, *Pick the bean to inject*.

spring-creation-order.title: Constructor injection order and cycle detection
spring-creation-order.description:
With constructor injection a bean cannot be built until every constructor argument exists. The container
therefore walks the definitions **in the order they were registered** and, before building a bean, first builds
each of its dependencies **in parameter order** (a depth-first walk). Every bean is a singleton: once built it is
reused.

`creation_order(beans)` receives a list of `[name, [dependency names]]` pairs. Every dependency name is the name
of a bean in the list.

- If all beans can be built, return `{"order": [...]}` with the names in the order their constructors finish.
- If the walk reaches a bean that is *currently being built*, there is a circular dependency. Return
  `{"cycle": [...]}` with the chain from that bean back to itself, for example `["a", "b", "a"]`. Report the
  first cycle the walk meets and stop.

**Example:** `[["controller", ["service"]], ["repo", []], ["service", ["repo"]]]` →
`{"order": ["repo", "service", "controller"]}`.

**Example:** `[["a", ["b"]], ["b", ["a"]]]` → `{"cycle": ["a", "b", "a"]}`.

guide.prereqs: Recursion and depth-first search. Lesson: *Circular dependencies, @Primary and @Qualifier*.
guide.intuition: Keep two collections: beans that are finished, and beans whose constructor is *waiting* for arguments right now. Meeting a waiting bean again means the chain has closed into a loop.
hints: Write a recursive `create(name)` that builds dependencies first and appends the name last.
A finished bean is skipped. A bean that is still on the 'in creation' list is a cycle.
The in-creation list is ordered, so the cycle is the slice from the repeated name to the end, plus the name.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly scan for a bean whose dependencies are all built (O(n²)); if a pass builds nothing, there is a cycle. That finds *whether* a cycle exists but not the order Spring would use.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E): each bean is built once and each dependency edge is followed once. Space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Using a single 'seen' set reports a diamond as a cycle. Forgetting to remove a bean from the in-creation list when it finishes has the same effect. A bean depending on itself is a cycle of length one.
guide.follow_up: Topological sort with Kahn's algorithm gives *an* order, but not necessarily the depth-first one.

spring-resolve-candidate.title: Pick the bean to inject: @Primary, @Qualifier and names
spring-resolve-candidate.description:
Several beans may share a type. Spring then needs a tie-breaker. Implement the decision for a single injection
point.

`resolve(candidates, required_type, qualifier, param_name)`:

- `candidates` — list of `{"name", "types", "primary"}` dicts (every bean in the context),
- `required_type` — the parameter's type,
- `qualifier` — the value of `@Qualifier` on the parameter, or `None`,
- `param_name` — the name of the constructor parameter.

Rules, in this order:

1. Keep only beans whose `types` contain `required_type`. None left → return `"NoSuchBeanDefinitionException"`.
2. If `qualifier` is given, the answer is the remaining bean whose **name equals the qualifier**; if there is none,
   return `"NoSuchBeanDefinitionException"`. (`@Primary` is ignored in this case.)
3. Exactly one bean left → that bean.
4. Exactly one of them is primary → that bean. More than one primary → `"NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException"`.
5. No primary: if a bean's name equals `param_name`, pick it. Otherwise `"NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException"`.

Return the chosen bean's name or the exception name.

**Example:** beans `emailNotifier` and `smsNotifier` both of type `Notifier`, none primary, no qualifier,
parameter named `notifier` → `"NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException"`; parameter named `smsNotifier` → `"smsNotifier"`.
spring-resolve-candidate.starter:
def resolve(candidates: list, required_type: str, qualifier, param_name: str) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Circular dependencies, @Primary and @Qualifier*. Python list comprehensions.
guide.intuition: The container narrows a list. Type narrows it first. An explicit qualifier is the strongest statement the developer can make; a primary flag is a default; the parameter name is the last resort.
hints: Start by filtering on type, and return early when the filtered list is empty.
Treat the qualifier branch completely separately: it either finds a name or fails.
Count primaries: one wins, several is ambiguous, zero falls through to the parameter-name comparison.
guide.brute_force: There is no cheaper or dearer algorithm here: the work is a linear filter. The difficulty is the order of the rules.
guide.complexity: Time O(n · t) to filter n beans with t types each. Space O(n) for the filtered list.
guide.pitfalls: Checking `@Primary` before the qualifier, or the parameter name before `@Primary`, both give plausible but wrong answers. A qualifier naming a bean of a *different* type must not match. Two primaries are an error, not 'first one wins'.
guide.follow_up: Real Spring also lets you inject `List<Notifier>` to receive every candidate. How would you add that?

spring-scope-count.title: Count instances: singleton versus prototype
spring-scope-count.description:
A **singleton** bean has one instance per container. A **prototype** bean gets a fresh instance every time
someone asks the container for it, including every time it is injected into another bean that is being created.

`count_instances(defs, gets)`:

- `defs` — list of `[name, scope, deps]` where `scope` is `"singleton"` or `"prototype"` and `deps` are the names
  of the beans injected into it when an instance is created. The graph has no cycles.
- `gets` — a list of bean names requested with `context.getBean(name)` after start-up, in order.

At start-up the container creates every singleton in definition order (dependencies are obtained first as needed).
Prototypes are created only on demand. *Obtaining* a singleton creates it the first time and reuses it afterwards;
*obtaining* a prototype always creates a new instance, and creating any instance obtains each of its `deps`.

Return a dict `name -> number of instances created`.

**Example:** `defs = [["cart", "prototype", ["catalog"]], ["catalog", "singleton", []]]`, `gets = ["cart", "cart"]`
→ `{"cart": 2, "catalog": 1}`.
spring-scope-count.starter:
def count_instances(defs: list, gets: list) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Singleton scope, eager and lazy beans, thread safety*. Recursion.
guide.intuition: 'Obtain' is the only operation. For a singleton it is create-once-then-reuse; for a prototype it is always create. Creating anything obtains its dependencies, so prototypes cascade.
hints: Write one helper, `obtain(name)`, and call it for start-up and for every `getBean`.
Remember which singletons exist in a set. Return early when a singleton is already there.
A prototype injected into a singleton is created once, at the moment the singleton is created.
guide.brute_force: Simulating the container literally, as described, is the straightforward solution. A closed formula exists (multiply counts along paths) but is harder to get right.
guide.complexity: Time O(total instances created × average dependency count). Space O(number of beans + recursion depth).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the eager start-up pass undercounts singletons nobody asks for. Assuming a prototype inside a singleton is recreated on each call is the classic interview trap: it is injected once.
guide.follow_up: How would `ObjectProvider<Cart>` or `@Lookup` change the count for the checkout example?

spring-lazy-eager-order.title: Eager and lazy initialisation order
spring-lazy-eager-order.description:
Singleton beans are **eager** by default: the container creates them while it starts. A bean marked `@Lazy` is
created only when something first needs it, and "something" can be another bean's constructor.

`init_log(defs, requests)`:

- `defs` — list of `{"name", "lazy", "deps"}` in registration order. All beans are singletons and the graph is acyclic.
- `requests` — bean names asked for with `getBean` after start-up.

Start-up: go through `defs` in order; for each bean that is **not lazy** and not created yet, create it. Creating a
bean first creates each of its not-yet-created `deps` in order (lazy or not), then the bean itself.
Afterwards serve `requests` in order, creating on first use with the same dependencies-first rule.

Return `{"startup": [...], "runtime": [...]}` listing bean names in creation order for each phase.

**Example:** `report` (lazy) depends on `clock`; `clock` is eager; requests `["report", "report"]` →
`{"startup": ["clock"], "runtime": ["report"]}`.
spring-lazy-eager-order.starter:
def init_log(defs: list, requests: list) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Singleton scope, eager and lazy beans, thread safety*. The previous problem on creation order.
guide.intuition: `@Lazy` on a class only says 'do not create me for my own sake at start-up'. If an eager bean needs it as a constructor argument, it has to exist, so it is created anyway.
hints: Reuse the dependencies-first recursion from the creation-order problem.
Pass the log list into the helper so the same code serves both phases.
Start-up loops only over non-lazy definitions, but the recursion ignores the lazy flag.
guide.brute_force: A two-list simulation is the solution; there is no slower alternative worth describing.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E + R) for V beans, E dependency edges and R requests. Space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Logging the bean before its dependencies reverses constructor order. Skipping lazy dependencies of eager beans is the misconception this problem exists to remove.
guide.follow_up: `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` makes every bean lazy. Which bugs would then surface only at runtime?

spring-lifecycle-order.title: Bean lifecycle callback order
spring-lifecycle-order.description:
After the container constructs a bean it runs the bean's initialisation callbacks, and when the context closes it
runs destruction callbacks. Produce the complete log.

`lifecycle(beans)` receives a list of dicts in registration order:

- `name`, `deps` (constructor dependencies, acyclic),
- `scope` — `"singleton"` or `"prototype"`,
- `callbacks` — any subset of `"postConstruct"`, `"afterPropertiesSet"`, `"initMethod"`, `"preDestroy"`,
  `"destroy"`, `"destroyMethod"`, in any order.

**Start-up.** For each singleton in registration order (if not created yet): obtain its dependencies in order, then
log `"<name>:constructor"`, then its initialisation callbacks that are present, always in the order
`postConstruct`, `afterPropertiesSet`, `initMethod`. Obtaining a singleton that exists does nothing. Obtaining a
prototype always builds a new instance in the same way (dependencies, constructor, init callbacks). A prototype
that nobody depends on is never built.

**Shutdown.** Log `"context:close"`. Then for each **singleton** in the reverse of the order their constructors
ran, log its destruction callbacks that are present in the order `preDestroy`, `destroy`, `destroyMethod`.
Prototype instances never receive destruction callbacks.

Return the list of log lines, each formatted `"<name>:<event>"`.

**Example:** one singleton `pool` with callbacks `["destroy", "postConstruct"]` →
`["pool:constructor", "pool:postConstruct", "context:close", "pool:destroy"]`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Prototype scope and the bean lifecycle*. The creation-order problem.
guide.intuition: Initialisation follows dependencies (what I need is ready before me); destruction is the mirror image (I shut down before the things I rely on). Within one bean the three callback styles have a fixed order.
hints: Keep a list, not a set, of created singletons: its order is needed again at shutdown.
Loop over the fixed order `postConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, initMethod` and test membership, rather than looping over the input list.
Prototype instances are never remembered, so they cannot appear in the shutdown phase.
guide.brute_force: Direct simulation is the intended solution.
guide.complexity: Time O(instances × callbacks). Space O(number of singletons).
guide.pitfalls: Emitting callbacks in the order they are listed in the input; destroying in creation order instead of reverse; calling destroy callbacks on prototypes, which Spring never does because it does not track them.
guide.follow_up: Where do `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization` and `…AfterInitialization` fit? (Around the three init callbacks; proxies are created in the 'after' step.)

spring-component-scan.title: Component scanning: which classes become beans?
spring-component-scan.description:
`@ComponentScan` tells Spring which packages to search for annotated classes. Model that search.

`scan(base_packages, classes)`:

- `base_packages` — list of package names such as `"com.bookshop"`,
- `classes` — list of `[fully_qualified_class_name, [annotations]]`, for example
  `["com.bookshop.web.CartController", ["RestController"]]`.

A class becomes a bean when **both** hold:

1. its package is one of the base packages or a **sub-package** of one (`com.bookshop.web` is inside
   `com.bookshop`; `com.bookshopping` is not), and
2. it carries at least one stereotype annotation: `Component`, `Service`, `Repository`, `Controller`,
   `RestController` or `Configuration`.

The bean name is the simple class name with its first letter lower-cased, **except** when the first two characters
are both upper-case, in which case the name is left unchanged (`URLShortener` stays `URLShortener`).

Return the bean names sorted alphabetically (plain `sorted`).

**Example:** base `["com.bookshop"]`, classes `com.bookshop.web.CartController` (`RestController`) and
`com.other.Tool` (`Component`) → `["cartController"]`.
spring-component-scan.starter:
def scan(base_packages: list, classes: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Stereotype annotations, component scanning and programmatic registration*. String methods.
guide.intuition: Two filters and a rename. The package filter must respect dots: a sub-package starts with the base package *followed by a dot*.
hints: Split the fully qualified name at the last dot to get package and simple name.
`package == base or package.startswith(base + '.')` avoids matching `com.bookshopping`.
The naming rule follows the JavaBeans convention: two leading capitals mean 'acronym, leave it alone'.
guide.brute_force: The scan is linear already. A naive `startswith(base)` is the tempting shortcut and is wrong.
guide.complexity: Time O(C · B) for C classes and B base packages, plus O(C log C) to sort. Space O(C).
guide.pitfalls: Prefix matching without the dot; forgetting that `@Entity` or a plain class is not a bean; lower-casing `URLShortener` to `uRLShortener`.
guide.follow_up: Add `excludeFilters` support, or meta-annotations (an annotation that is itself annotated with `@Component`).

spring-conditional-autoconfig.title: Auto-configuration: evaluate the conditions
spring-conditional-autoconfig.description:
Spring Boot's auto-configuration is a list of configuration classes, each guarded by **conditions**. Boot evaluates
them after your own beans are registered and adds a bean only when every condition passes.

`evaluate(configs, classpath, user_beans, properties)`:

- `configs` — ordered list of `{"name", "bean", "conditions"}`; `bean` is the bean name the configuration would add.
- `classpath` — list of class names present.
- `user_beans` — bean names the application defined itself.
- `properties` — dict of configuration properties (string values).

Conditions are checked left to right; the first failing one decides:

| condition | passes when |
|---|---|
| `["onClass", c]` | `c` is on the classpath |
| `["onMissingClass", c]` | `c` is not on the classpath |
| `["onBean", b]` | a bean named `b` is registered so far |
| `["onMissingBean", b]` | no bean named `b` is registered so far |
| `["onProperty", key, having, match_if_missing]` | key absent → `match_if_missing`. Key present and `having` is `None` → the value is anything except `"false"` (case-insensitive). Otherwise the value equals `having` (case-insensitive) |

"Registered so far" means the user beans plus beans added by earlier configurations in the list.

Return `{"beans": [...], "report": [...]}` where `beans` is user beans followed by auto-configured beans in the
order they were added, and `report` has one `[config_name, verdict]` pair per configuration: `"matched"` or the
failing condition written as `"<kind>:<first argument>"`, e.g. `"onMissingBean:dataSource"`.
spring-conditional-autoconfig.starter:
def evaluate(configs: list, classpath: list, user_beans: list, properties: dict) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Spring Boot: starters and auto-configuration*.
guide.intuition: Auto-configuration is 'if nobody has supplied this already and the library is present, I will'. Each condition is a yes/no question about the classpath, the bean registry or the properties.
hints: Keep one growing list of registered bean names, seeded with the user's beans.
Write a helper that answers one condition; the loop then only needs to find the first `False`.
For `onProperty` handle 'key absent' first; only then look at `having`.
guide.brute_force: A straight loop is the solution. The care is in `onProperty` and in using the *growing* bean list.
guide.complexity: Time O(total conditions × lookup cost). Using sets for the classpath and beans makes each lookup O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Checking bean conditions against only the user's beans misses chains such as JdbcTemplate needing the auto-configured DataSource. `havingValue` unset does not mean 'must be true': any value except `false` passes.
guide.follow_up: Real Boot orders configurations with `@AutoConfigureAfter`/`@AutoConfigureBefore`. Add a topological sort in front.

spring-property-precedence.title: Which property source wins?
spring-property-precedence.description:
Spring Boot reads configuration from several places and lets later, more specific places override earlier ones.
For this problem there are five sources, from **lowest to highest** priority:

1. `defaults` — defaults set in code,
2. `application` — `application.properties`,
3. `profiles` — `application-<profile>.properties` for each **active** profile; when several active profiles
   define the key, the profile listed **last** in `active_profiles` wins,
4. `env` — operating-system environment variables,
5. `args` — command-line arguments such as `--server.port=9000`.

Environment variables cannot contain dots or dashes, so Boot uses *relaxed binding*: to find the variable for a
key, replace every `.` with `_`, delete every `-`, and upper-case the result (`shop.page-size` → `SHOP_PAGESIZE`).

`resolve_property(key, sources, active_profiles)` receives `sources` as a dict with exactly those five entries
(`profiles` maps a profile name to its dict). Return `[value, label]` for the winning source, where the label is
`"args"`, `"env"`, `"profile:<name>"`, `"application"` or `"defaults"`. Return `None` if no source has the key.
A profile that is not active is ignored.

**Example:** `server.port` is `8080` in defaults, `8081` in application and `9000` in args → `["9000", "args"]`.
spring-property-precedence.starter:
def resolve_property(key: str, sources: dict, active_profiles: list):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Configuration properties, profiles and logging*. Python dict lookups.
guide.intuition: The closer a setting is to the moment of launch, the more it should count: a file packed into the jar loses to the environment of the machine, which loses to what the operator typed on the command line.
hints: Check the sources from highest priority to lowest and return at the first hit.
Convert the key to its environment-variable spelling before looking in `env`.
Walk `active_profiles` backwards so the last active profile is consulted first.
guide.brute_force: Merge all dicts from lowest to highest into one and look the key up. It works but loses the label unless you store it too, and it does needless work for one key.
guide.approach:
Probe in order `args → env → profiles (reversed) → application → defaults`.

**Dry run** for `shop.page-size` with `prod` active: not in args; env name is `SHOP_PAGESIZE`, present with
`100` → `["100", "env"]`. The `prod` profile's `50` and the file's `25` never get a look.

```properties
# src/main/resources/application.properties
shop.page-size=25
```

```bash
SHOP_PAGESIZE=100 java -jar bookshop.jar --server.port=9000 --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "shop")
public record ShopProperties(int pageSize, String title) { }   // pageSize == 100
```
guide.complexity: Time O(P) for P active profiles (every lookup is a hash probe). Space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Looking up the dotted key in the environment; letting the *first* active profile win; treating inactive profile files as if they were loaded.
guide.follow_up: The real list has around fifteen levels (config outside the jar beats config inside it, `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON`, test properties…). Extend the table.

spring-placeholder-expand.title: Expand ${placeholders} with defaults
spring-placeholder-expand.description:
Property values and `@Value` strings may contain placeholders. Implement the expansion.

`expand(text, props)` returns `text` with every placeholder replaced:

- `${key}` → the value of `key` in `props`. That value is expanded too (values may contain placeholders).
- `${key:default}` → the value of `key` if present, otherwise `default`. The default is everything after the
  **first** colon that is not inside a nested placeholder, may be empty, and is itself expanded.
- Placeholders nest: `${a:${b:none}}` and `${db.${env}.url}` are legal. Expand the key part first, then look it up.
- If a key is missing and there is no default, return the string
  `"ERROR: Could not resolve placeholder '<key>'"` (the whole result is that message).
- If expanding a key requires that same key again, return `"ERROR: Circular placeholder reference '<key>'"`,
  naming the key that was met for the second time.
- A `${` with no matching `}` is ordinary text. So is a lone `$` or `}`.

**Example:** `props = {"shop.name": "Bookshop"}`: `expand("Hi ${shop.name}!", props)` → `"Hi Bookshop!"`;
`expand("${port:8080}", props)` → `"8080"`.
spring-placeholder-expand.starter:
def expand(text: str, props: dict) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: String scanning with indexes, recursion. Lesson: *Configuration properties, profiles and logging*.
guide.intuition: A placeholder is a small expression with brackets that can nest, so a regular expression is not enough: you have to count opening `${` and closing `}` to find where each one ends, then recurse into the pieces.
hints: Scan left to right. On `${`, walk forward counting depth until it returns to zero; that is the matching brace.
Inside the braces, the key/default split is the first `:` seen while the nested depth is zero.
Carry a list of keys currently being expanded. Meeting one of them again is a cycle.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly replace the innermost `${...}` (one with no `$`, `{`, `}` inside) until none remain. It handles nesting but evaluates defaults that should never be touched and cannot name the key in a cycle.
guide.approach:
Recursive descent:

1. Copy ordinary characters.
2. At `${`, find the matching `}` by depth counting. No match → the rest is literal.
3. Split the inside into `key` and optional `default` at the first top-level colon.
4. Expand the key text itself (this is what makes `${db.${env}.url}` work).
5. Key known → expand its value with the key added to the *visiting* list. Key unknown → expand the default, or fail.

**Dry run** `${a:${b:none}}` with neither key defined: inner is `a:${b:none}`; key `a`, default `${b:none}`.
`a` is missing → expand the default → key `b`, default `none` → `none`.

Note that the default is only expanded when needed, so `${shop.name:${also.missing}}` succeeds.

```java
@Component
class ShopBanner {
    ShopBanner(@Value("${shop.greeting:Welcome}") String greeting,
               @Value("${shop.page-size:20}") int pageSize) { }   // text is converted to int after expansion
}
```
guide.complexity: Time O(L) per level of expansion, so O(total expanded length × nesting depth). Space O(depth) for the recursion.
guide.pitfalls: Splitting on the *last* colon breaks `${url:http://host:8080}`. Using `[^}]*` in a regex breaks nesting. Eagerly expanding defaults reports errors for values that are never used.
guide.follow_up: Spring also has `#{...}` (Spring Expression Language), which is evaluated *after* placeholders. Add arithmetic.

spring-advice-order.title: AOP advice ordering: build the call log
spring-advice-order.description:
Several aspects can intercept the same method. Each aspect may have up to five kinds of advice. Produce the log of
what runs, in order.

`call_log(aspects, outcome)`:

- `aspects` — list of `{"name", "order", "advices", "catches"}`. `advices` is a subset of `"around"`, `"before"`,
  `"afterReturning"`, `"afterThrowing"`, `"after"`. `catches` only matters when the aspect has `around`: it means
  the around advice wraps `proceed()` in try/catch and returns a fallback value.
- `outcome` — `"return"` or `"throw"`: what the target method does.

Rules:

1. Aspects are nested by `order`: the **lowest** number is the outermost. Ties are broken by name (alphabetical).
2. On the way **in**, each aspect from outermost to innermost logs `"<name>:around-before"` (if it has `around`)
   and then `"<name>:before"` (if it has `before`).
3. Then the target logs `"target:return"` or `"target:throw"`.
4. On the way **out**, each aspect from innermost to outermost sees the current outcome:
   - outcome is a normal return: `"<name>:afterReturning"`, `"<name>:after"`, `"<name>:around-after"`
     (each only if that advice exists);
   - outcome is an exception: `"<name>:afterThrowing"`, `"<name>:after"`, then, if the aspect has `around` **and**
     `catches`, `"<name>:around-recovered"` and the outcome becomes a normal return for all aspects further out.
     An around advice that does not catch logs nothing on the way out of an exception.

Return the list of log lines.

**Example:** one aspect `log` with `["around", "before", "after"]`, outcome `"return"` →
`["log:around-before", "log:before", "target:return", "log:after", "log:around-after"]`.
spring-advice-order.starter:
def call_log(aspects: list, outcome: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Advice types, pointcut expressions and aspect order*. Sorting with a key function.
guide.intuition: Picture Russian dolls. The lowest order number is the biggest doll. A call travels inwards through every doll to the target and the result (or exception) travels back out through the same dolls in reverse.
hints: Sort once by `(order, name)`; iterate forwards for the way in and backwards for the way out.
Keep a boolean 'an exception is travelling'. It starts from `outcome` and can only be switched off by a catching around advice.
Within one aspect on the way out: the returning/throwing advice first, then `after`, then the around tail.
guide.brute_force: You could build real nested Python closures, one per advice, and call them. It is a faithful model but much more code than two loops.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the two passes. Space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Unwinding in the same direction as entering; running `after` before `afterReturning` (the order inside one aspect changed in Spring Framework 5.2.7 and is now as in this problem); forgetting that a caught exception looks like a normal return to outer aspects.
guide.follow_up: A retry aspect calls `proceed()` more than once. How would the log look for 'fails twice, then succeeds'?

spring-pointcut-match.title: Match execution() pointcut expressions
spring-pointcut-match.description:
A pointcut expression selects the methods an aspect intercepts. Implement a matcher for this subset:

```
execution(<return> <type>.<method>(<params>))
```

- `<return>` — `*` (any) or a return type name. A `*` inside a name matches any run of letters/digits.
- `<type>` — a fully qualified class pattern, dot-separated. Inside a segment `*` matches any run of
  letters, digits and `_` (possibly empty). The token `..` between segments matches the dot plus **zero or more
  whole package segments**: `com.bookshop..*` is any class in `com.bookshop` or any sub-package.
- `<method>` — the method name, `*` allowed as in a segment. The method name is the part after the last dot
  before `(`.
- `<params>` — comma-separated list. `..` matches zero or more parameters of any type, `*` matches exactly one
  parameter of any type, anything else must equal the parameter type. An empty list `()` matches only methods
  without parameters.

`matches(expression, methods)` receives the expression and a list of method descriptions
`{"ret", "cls", "name", "params"}` (`cls` is fully qualified). Return a list of booleans, one per method.

**Example:** `execution(* com.bookshop.service.*.*(..))` matches every method of every class directly in
`com.bookshop.service`, but not `com.bookshop.service.order.OrderService.findOrders`.
spring-pointcut-match.starter:
def matches(expression: str, methods: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Regular expressions, recursion. Lesson: *Advice types, pointcut expressions and aspect order*.
guide.intuition: The expression has four slots: return type, class, method name, parameters. Three of them are text globs that translate neatly into regular expressions; the parameter list is a small sequence-matching problem of its own.
hints: Pull the four slots apart first. The method name is whatever follows the last dot before the bracket.
Translate a type pattern piece by piece: `..` → a dot followed by zero or more `segment.` groups; `*` → `\w*`; everything else escaped.
For parameters, when the pattern head is `..` try letting it swallow 0, 1, 2… actual parameters and recurse on the rest.
guide.brute_force: Hand-write comparisons for the handful of shapes you expect (`(..)`, `()`, exact). That passes simple cases and collapses on `(String, ..)` or `(.., boolean)`.
guide.complexity: Regex matching is linear in the class name for these patterns. The parameter matcher is O(p · a) with memoisation, exponential without only when many `..` appear; real signatures are short.
guide.pitfalls: Treating `..` as 'any characters' lets `com.bookshop..*` match `com.bookshopping.X`. Letting `*` cross a dot makes `com.bookshop.*.*` match deeper packages. `()` is not the same as `(..)`.
guide.follow_up: Add `within(...)`, `@annotation(...)` and the combinators `&&`, `||`, `!`.

spring-self-invocation.title: Detect proxy self-invocation
spring-self-invocation.description:
Spring applies `@Transactional` (and every other aspect) through a **proxy** that stands in front of your object.
Only calls that go *through the proxy* are intercepted. A method that calls another method of the same object with
`this.other()` skips the proxy, so the annotation on `other` does nothing. This is the *self-invocation pitfall*.

`trace(methods, entry)`:

- `methods` — dict `name -> {"transactional": bool, "calls": [[via, name], ...]}` describing one service class.
  `via` is `"this"` (a direct call on the same object) or `"proxy"` (a call through the Spring-managed reference,
  for example a self-injected bean or another bean calling back).
- `entry` — the method an outside caller invokes. Outside callers always go through the proxy.

Follow the calls depth-first in the listed order (the call graph has no cycles) and return one `[method, verdict]`
pair per invocation, in the order the invocations start:

- `"advised"` — the method is transactional and was reached through the proxy,
- `"bypassed"` — the method is transactional but was reached through `this`,
- `"plain"` — the method is not transactional.

**Example:** `placeOrder` (not transactional) calls `this.reserveStock` (transactional) →
`[["placeOrder", "plain"], ["reserveStock", "bypassed"]]`.
spring-self-invocation.starter:
def trace(methods: dict, entry: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *How Spring AOP works: proxies and your first aspect* and *@Transactional, rollback rules and the self-invocation pitfall*.
guide.intuition: The verdict depends on exactly two facts: is the method annotated, and which door did this particular call come through. Nothing about the caller's own status matters.
hints: Carry the `via` of the current call as a parameter of your recursive function.
The entry call counts as `proxy`.
Record the verdict before descending into the callees so the output is in start order.
guide.brute_force: The recursion is the direct solution; the mistake to avoid is making it smarter than the rule.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(number of invocations).
guide.pitfalls: Marking every annotated method as advised; 'inheriting' the bypass from the caller; recording the verdict after the children (post-order).
guide.follow_up: Private and `final` methods cannot be overridden by a class-based proxy. Add a `visibility` field and report those too.

spring-request-mapping.title: Resolve a request to a handler method
spring-request-mapping.description:
`DispatcherServlet` asks its handler mapping which controller method should serve a request. Implement that
decision.

`resolve(mappings, method, path)`:

- `mappings` — list of `{"pattern", "methods", "handler"}`. An empty `methods` list means *any HTTP method*.
- `method` — e.g. `"GET"`. `path` — starts with `/`, no query string.

**Matching.** Split pattern and path on `/` into segments (the root `/` has zero segments). Segment by segment:

- literal text must be equal (case-sensitive),
- `{name}` matches exactly one non-empty segment and captures it (as a string),
- `*` matches exactly one non-empty segment without capturing,
- `**` appears only as the final pattern segment and matches all remaining segments (zero or more).

Apart from `**`, the number of segments must be equal. A trailing slash is significant: `/books/` does not match
`/books` (the Spring Framework 6 default).

**Choosing.**

1. No pattern matches the path → `[404, None, {}]`.
2. Patterns match the path but none of them allows the method → `[405, None, {}]`.
3. Otherwise, among mappings that match path and method, the **most specific** wins: fewest `**`; then fewest
   one-segment wildcards (`{name}` and `*` counted together); then most literal segments. The input never
   contains a tie.

Return `[200, handler, variables]`.

**Example:** `GET /books/featured` matches both `/books/{id}` and `/books/featured`; the literal one wins →
`[200, "featuredBooks", {}]`. `DELETE /books/7` → `[405, None, {}]`.
spring-request-mapping.starter:
def resolve(mappings: list, method: str, path: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lessons: *Spring MVC: the request flow through DispatcherServlet* and *Request parameters, path variables and the Model*.
guide.intuition: Two separate questions: *which patterns fit this path?* and *of those that also accept the method, which is the least vague?* Keeping them separate is what lets you tell 404 from 405.
hints: Write `match(pattern, path)` returning a dict of variables or `None`. Compare segment lists, not strings.
Track a flag 'some pattern matched the path' independently of the method check.
Specificity is a tuple you can compare directly: `(count of **, count of single wildcards, -literal count)`.
guide.brute_force: Return the first mapping that matches. It is O(n) too, but registration order then decides between `/books/{id}` and `/books/featured`, which Spring never does.
guide.complexity: Time O(M · S) for M mappings and S path segments. Space O(S).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing whole strings instead of segments; answering 404 where 405 is correct; letting `{id}` match an empty segment so `/books/` hits `getBook`; forgetting that `/files/**` also matches `/files`.
guide.follow_up: Spring also narrows by `consumes`, `produces`, `params` and `headers`. Add `produces` using the content-negotiation problem.

spring-param-binding.title: Bind and convert request parameters
spring-param-binding.description:
A controller method declares `@RequestParam` arguments; Spring reads the query string, converts the text to the
declared types and reports a `400 Bad Request` when it cannot.

`bind(spec, query)`:

- `spec` — list of `{"name", "type", "required", "default"}` in parameter order. `type` is one of `"String"`,
  `"int"`, `"boolean"`, `"double"`, `"int[]"`. `default` is a string or `None`.
- `query` — the raw query string without `?`, e.g. `"q=dune&page=2"`. Pairs are separated by `&`; a pair without
  `=` has the empty string as value; `+` means space and `%XX` is percent-decoding (apply to names and values).
  Empty pairs are ignored. Parameters not in the spec are ignored.

For each parameter in order:

1. Take the **first** value given for the name. For `int[]` take *all* values, split each on commas, and drop
   empty pieces.
2. If there is no value — or the value is the empty string and the type is not `String` (for `int[]`: no pieces
   left) — use `default` instead (for `int[]`, split it on commas).
3. Still nothing: when `required`, fail with `"Required request parameter '<name>' is not present"`; otherwise
   the argument is `None` (`[]` for `int[]`).
4. Convert. `int`: optional sign and digits. `double`: optional sign, digits with optional fraction, optional
   exponent (`1e3`, `.5`, `2.` are fine; `abc`, `1,5`, `inf` are not). `boolean`: `true/on/yes/1` → `True`,
   `false/off/no/0` → `False`, ignoring case. On failure:
   `"Failed to convert parameter '<name>' with value '<text>' to <type>"` (for arrays: the offending piece, type `int`).

Return `{"status": 200, "args": {...}}`, or `{"status": 400, "error": message}` for the **first** failing parameter.
spring-param-binding.starter:
def bind(spec: list, query: str) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Request parameters, path variables and the Model*. String splitting, `try/except`.
guide.intuition: Three stages per parameter: *find* the text, *fall back* to a default or complain, *convert*. Errors are data here: the function reports the first one instead of crashing.
hints: Parse the query string once into `name -> list of values`, decoding as you go.
Decide the text to convert before thinking about types; an empty string counts as absent for non-String types.
Raise a private exception from the converter and catch it once, turning it into the 400 result.
guide.brute_force: `dict(pair.split('=') ...)` plus `int(text)` handles the happy path. It loses repeated parameters, crashes on pairs without `=`, skips URL decoding and accepts `int(' 7 ')` or `float('inf')`.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the query + number of parameters). Space O(length of the query).
guide.pitfalls: Using Python's permissive `int()`/`float()` (they accept spaces, underscores, `inf`, `nan`); treating a supplied default as making the parameter optional *and* still reporting it missing; decoding `+` after splitting on it; reading the last instead of the first repeated value.
guide.follow_up: Bind onto an object instead (`@ModelAttribute`), collecting *all* errors in a `BindingResult`.

spring-bean-validation.title: Bean Validation: collect field errors
spring-bean-validation.description:
With `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody`, Spring runs Jakarta Bean Validation and answers `400` with the list of
violations. Implement the checker.

`validate(constraints, obj)`:

- `constraints` — dict `field -> list of rules`. A rule is a list whose first item is the constraint name.
- `obj` — dict of the submitted values. A missing field counts as `None`.

| rule | passes when | message |
|---|---|---|
| `["NotNull"]` | value is not `None` | `must not be null` |
| `["NotBlank"]` | a string containing at least one non-whitespace character | `must not be blank` |
| `["NotEmpty"]` | a string or list with length > 0 | `must not be empty` |
| `["Size", min, max]` | `min <= len(value) <= max` (string or list) | `size must be between {min} and {max}` |
| `["Min", n]` | `value >= n` | `must be greater than or equal to {n}` |
| `["Max", n]` | `value <= n` | `must be less than or equal to {n}` |
| `["Positive"]` | `value > 0` | `must be greater than 0` |
| `["Email"]` | empty string, or text of the form `something@something` with no spaces and exactly one `@` | `must be a well-formed email address` |
| `["Pattern", regex]` | the **whole** string matches the regular expression | `must match "{regex}"` |

Important: `None` **passes** every rule except `NotNull`, `NotBlank` and `NotEmpty`. That is how Bean Validation
works: "optional but, if present, valid".

Report every violation. Return `{"status": 200, "errors": []}` when there are none, otherwise
`{"status": 400, "errors": [[field, message], ...]}` ordered by field name (alphabetical) and, within a field, by
the order of its rules.
spring-bean-validation.starter:
def validate(constraints: dict, obj: dict) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Request bodies, validation and error handling with @RestControllerAdvice*.
guide.intuition: Each constraint is a tiny yes/no function of one value. The framework's job is bookkeeping: run them all, never stop at the first failure, and report which field each message belongs to.
hints: Write one function that takes a rule and a value and returns a message or `None`.
Handle the three 'presence' rules first, then return 'pass' for `None`, then the rest.
`re.fullmatch` mirrors Java's `String.matches`, which must consume the whole input.
guide.brute_force: A long chain of `if` statements per field works for one class and has to be rewritten for the next. The table-driven version is the point of the exercise.
guide.complexity: Time O(total rules × cost of each check). Space O(number of violations).
guide.pitfalls: Failing null values on `@Size`, `@Min`, `@Email` (they are valid; add `@NotNull` if the field is mandatory). Using `re.match`, which accepts a prefix. Stopping at the first error per field.
guide.follow_up: Add nested validation (`@Valid` on a field containing another object) with paths such as `address.zip`.

spring-exception-status.title: Map an exception to an HTTP status
spring-exception-status.description:
When a controller throws, Spring MVC looks for an `@ExceptionHandler` method that fits, and failing that for a
`@ResponseStatus` annotation on the exception class. Reproduce the lookup.

`resolve_status(parents, handlers, annotated, thrown)`:

- `parents` — dict `class -> parent class` (`None` for the root `Throwable`),
- `handlers` — list of `[exception_class, status]` pairs from a `@RestControllerAdvice`,
- `annotated` — dict `exception_class -> status` for classes carrying `@ResponseStatus`,
- `thrown` — the class of the exception that was thrown.

Rules:

1. Walk from `thrown` up through its ancestors. The **first** class that has a handler wins (the closest
   ancestor, with distance 0 for the class itself) → `[status, "handler:<class>"]`.
2. If no handler applies, walk up again and use the first class found in `annotated` →
   `[status, "annotation:<class>"]`.
3. Otherwise → `[500, "default"]`.

**Example:** handlers for `ShopException → 422` and `Exception → 500`; throwing `OutOfStockException` (a subclass
of `ShopException`) → `[422, "handler:ShopException"]`.
spring-exception-status.starter:
def resolve_status(parents: dict, handlers: list, annotated: dict, thrown: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Java inheritance (the Java track's exceptions lesson). Lesson: *Request bodies, validation and error handling with @RestControllerAdvice*.
guide.intuition: A handler for `ShopException` also covers its subclasses, but a handler written for the exact subclass is a better fit. 'Better fit' means fewer steps up the family tree.
hints: First build the list `[thrown, parent, grandparent, ..., Throwable]`.
Turn the handler pairs into a dict so each ancestor check is one lookup.
Do the two passes separately: all handlers are considered before any annotation.
guide.brute_force: For every handler compute the distance from `thrown` by walking up, and keep the minimum: O(H · D). Walking the lineage once with a dict is O(H + D).
guide.complexity: Time O(H + D) for H handlers and inheritance depth D. Space O(H + D).
guide.pitfalls: Taking the first handler in declaration order instead of the closest one; mixing the two passes so an annotation on a subclass beats a handler on a superclass; forgetting distance 0.
guide.follow_up: Real Spring also unwraps `getCause()` when no handler matches the outer exception, and prefers handlers inside the controller over advice classes.

spring-content-negotiation.title: Content negotiation with the Accept header
spring-content-negotiation.description:
A client says which response formats it understands with the `Accept` header; the server picks one it can
produce. Implement the choice.

`negotiate(accept, produces)`:

- `accept` — the header value, e.g. `"text/csv;q=0.5, application/*, */*;q=0.1"`, or `None`/empty when absent
  (treat that as `*/*`).
- `produces` — the concrete media types the handler can write, in the server's order of preference.

Steps:

1. Split the header on commas. Each entry is a media range optionally followed by `;`-separated parameters; only
   the `q` parameter matters (a number from 0 to 1, default 1). Ignore surrounding spaces; compare
   case-insensitively (work in lower case). Drop entries with `q = 0`.
2. Sort the entries: higher `q` first; for equal `q`, more specific first (`type/subtype`, then `type/*`, then
   `*/*`); remaining ties keep header order.
3. Go through the sorted entries. For each, scan `produces` in order and return the first type compatible with
   the entry: `*/*` accepts anything, `type/*` accepts the same type, otherwise the types must be equal.
4. Nothing compatible → return `"406 Not Acceptable"`.

Return the chosen media type exactly as written in `produces`.

**Example:** `negotiate("application/xml, application/json;q=0.9", ["application/json", "application/xml"])` →
`"application/xml"`.
spring-content-negotiation.starter:
def negotiate(accept, produces: list) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: HTTP headers (the networking track or the lesson *REST endpoints with @RestController and ResponseEntity*). Sorting by a tuple.
guide.intuition: The client ranks what it wants, the server ranks what it has. Walk the client's ranking from the top and stop at the first thing the server can deliver.
hints: Parse each entry into `(q, specificity, position, media range)`.
Sort by `(-q, specificity, position)` so a plain `sorted` gives the right order.
Write the compatibility test for the three shapes `*/*`, `type/*`, `type/subtype` separately.
guide.brute_force: Ignore `q` and take header order. Browsers send `*/*;q=0.8` in the middle of the header, so this picks the wrong format regularly.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** for `text/csv;q=0.5, application/*, */*;q=0.1` with JSON, XML, CSV on offer. Sorted entries:
`application/*` (q 1), `text/csv` (0.5), `*/*` (0.1). The first entry is compatible with `application/json`,
the server's first preference → JSON.

```java
@GetMapping(value = "/books/{id}",
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE})
Book getBook(@PathVariable long id) { ... }
```

```bash
curl -H "Accept: application/xml" http://localhost:8080/books/7     # XML if a converter is on the classpath
curl -H "Accept: image/png"       http://localhost:8080/books/7     # 406 Not Acceptable
```
guide.complexity: Time O(A log A + A · P) for A accept entries and P producible types. Space O(A).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the default `q=1`; comparing case-sensitively; returning the client's wildcard (`application/*`) instead of a concrete type; keeping `q=0` entries.
guide.follow_up: Spring can also negotiate with a `?format=xml` parameter. Where would that slot into the algorithm?

spring-tx-propagation.title: Transaction propagation over a call tree
spring-tx-propagation.description:
Every `@Transactional` method declares a **propagation**: what to do about a transaction that may already be
running. Simulate a tree of calls and report which rows end up in the database.

`run(root)` receives a node `{"name", "propagation", "fails", "caught", "calls"}`:

- When a method's body runs it first **writes one row** named after the method, then calls each node in `calls`
  in order, and finally throws `RuntimeException` if `fails` is true.
- `caught` (ignored on the root) says the *caller* wraps this call in try/catch and carries on. Uncaught
  exceptions travel up to the caller's caller.
- A write made inside a transaction becomes permanent only if that transaction commits. A write made with no
  transaction is permanent immediately (auto-commit).

Propagation, with *T* = the transaction active in the caller (possibly none):

| value | T exists | no T |
|---|---|---|
| `REQUIRED` | join T | start a new transaction |
| `SUPPORTS` | join T | run without a transaction |
| `MANDATORY` | join T | throw `IllegalTransactionStateException` before the body |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | suspend T, start an independent new transaction | start a new transaction |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED` | suspend T, run without a transaction | run without a transaction |
| `NEVER` | throw `IllegalTransactionStateException` before the body | run without a transaction |
| `NESTED` | take a savepoint in T | start a new transaction |

Boundaries:

- **A method that started a transaction**: if an exception leaves its body, the transaction rolls back and the
  exception continues upward. Otherwise it commits — unless the transaction was marked *rollback-only*, in which
  case it rolls back and the method throws `UnexpectedRollbackException` to its caller.
- **A method that joined T**: if an exception leaves its body, T is marked rollback-only and the exception
  continues upward (even if the caller then catches it, T is doomed).
- **NESTED with a savepoint**: if an exception leaves the body, every row T gained since the savepoint is removed,
  the rollback-only mark is restored to what it was at the savepoint, and the exception continues upward.

Return `{"rows": [...], "error": ...}`: the permanent rows in the order they were written, and the name of the
exception that escapes the root (`None` if none).

**Example:** `checkout` (REQUIRED) calls `audit` (REQUIRES_NEW), then fails →
`{"rows": ["audit"], "error": "RuntimeException"}`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons: *@Transactional, rollback rules and the self-invocation pitfall* and *Propagation and isolation*. Python exceptions and recursion.
guide.intuition: Separate two things: the *physical* transaction (a bag of uncommitted rows with a rollback-only flag) and the *methods* that either own it, borrow it, or stay out of it. Only the owner commits or rolls back; a borrower that fails can merely poison the bag.
hints: Model a transaction as an object with `rows` and `rollback_only`. Pass it (or `None`) down the recursion.
Write three helpers: run in a new transaction, run joined, run without one. `call` only chooses among them.
Global write order across independent transactions is easiest with a counter attached to every row; sort at the end.
guide.brute_force: Treat the whole tree as one transaction: everything commits or nothing does. It is right for all-REQUIRED trees with no caught exceptions and wrong for everything interesting.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(number of nodes).
guide.pitfalls: Believing that catching an exception saves a joined transaction; committing rows of a new transaction at the moment of writing instead of at its boundary; letting `MANDATORY`/`NEVER` write before throwing; marking the outer transaction rollback-only for a `NESTED` or `REQUIRES_NEW` failure.
guide.follow_up: Add `noRollbackFor`, or a checked exception that commits (see the rollback-rules problem).

spring-rollback-rules.title: Rollback rules: checked versus unchecked
spring-rollback-rules.description:
When an exception leaves a `@Transactional` method, Spring must decide between rollback and commit.

`decide(parents, thrown, rollback_for, no_rollback_for)`:

- `parents` — dict `class -> parent` describing the exception hierarchy (root `Throwable` has parent `None`),
- `thrown` — the exception class, or `None` if the method returned normally,
- `rollback_for`, `no_rollback_for` — lists of classes from the annotation's attributes.

Rules:

1. `thrown` is `None` → `"COMMIT"`.
2. A rule *applies* if its class is `thrown` or one of its ancestors. Its **distance** is the number of steps up
   (0 for the class itself). Among all applying rules from both lists, the one with the smallest distance wins:
   from `rollback_for` → `"ROLLBACK"`, from `no_rollback_for` → `"COMMIT"`. If the smallest distance is shared by
   a rule of each kind, rollback wins.
3. No rule applies → the default: `"ROLLBACK"` when `thrown` is `RuntimeException`, `Error`, or a descendant of
   either (the *unchecked* exceptions); `"COMMIT"` for everything else (the *checked* exceptions).

**Example:** throwing `IOException` with empty lists → `"COMMIT"` (checked). With
`rollback_for = ["Exception"]` → `"ROLLBACK"`.
spring-rollback-rules.starter:
def decide(parents: dict, thrown, rollback_for: list, no_rollback_for: list) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Checked and unchecked exceptions (Java track). Lesson: *@Transactional, rollback rules and the self-invocation pitfall*.
guide.intuition: The default follows an old convention: an unchecked exception signals a bug or an unrecoverable state, a checked exception is an expected business outcome. Explicit rules override that default, and the most specific rule is the one nearest to the thrown class.
hints: Compute `class -> distance` for the thrown class and all its ancestors in one walk.
Scan `rollback_for` first and replace the best only on a *strictly* smaller distance; ties then favour rollback.
The default needs the same ancestor map: is `RuntimeException` or `Error` in it?
guide.brute_force: Check `no_rollback_for` then `rollback_for` with simple membership. It ignores distance and fails whenever both lists contain ancestors of the thrown class.
guide.complexity: Time O(D + R) for hierarchy depth D and R rules. Space O(D).
guide.pitfalls: Assuming every exception rolls back (checked ones commit by default, the number-one `@Transactional` surprise); giving one list blanket priority over the other; forgetting `Error`.
guide.follow_up: An exception that is caught inside the method never reaches the proxy. What does the transaction do then?

spring-isolation-anomaly.title: Spot the isolation anomalies in a schedule
spring-isolation-anomaly.description:
Two or more transactions run at the same time; their operations interleave in a **schedule**. Decide which read
anomalies the schedule contains.

`anomalies(schedule)` receives a list of steps, each a list:

- `[tx, "read", key]`, `[tx, "write", key]` — read or update one row,
- `[tx, "scan", prefix]` — a range query returning every row whose key starts with `prefix`,
- `[tx, "insert", key]` — add a new row,
- `[tx, "commit"]`, `[tx, "rollback"]` — finish the transaction.

Let positions be indexes in the list, and A, B two **different** transactions. The schedule contains:

- **dirty read** — A reads `k` at position *i*, and B wrote or inserted `k` at some *j < i* without B committing
  or rolling back between *j* and *i*.
- **non-repeatable read** — A reads `k` at *i*; B writes `k` at *j > i*; B commits at *c > j*; A reads `k` again
  at *m > c*.
- **phantom read** — A scans prefix `p` at *i*; B inserts a key starting with `p` at *j > i*; B commits at
  *c > j*; A scans `p` again at *m > c*.
- **lost update** — A reads `k` at *i*; B writes `k` at *j > i*; B commits at *c > j*; A writes `k` at *m > c*
  **without** A reading `k` anywhere between *c* and *m*.

Return the names of the anomalies present, sorted alphabetically (each at most once).

**Example:** `[["T1","write","stock"], ["T2","read","stock"], ["T1","rollback"]]` → `["dirty read"]`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Propagation and isolation*. Nested loops over a list with indexes.
guide.intuition: Each anomaly is a fixed pattern of 'A did this, B did that in between, A looked again'. The definitions are already algorithms; the work is translating 'between' and 'committed' into index checks.
hints: Write two helpers: 'did transaction X finish between positions lo and hi?' and 'where does X commit after position j (if it does)?'.
Drive everything from A's first `read` (three anomalies start there) and A's first `scan`.
A rolled-back writer can cause a dirty read but never the other three, which all need B's commit.
guide.brute_force: The definitions give an O(n³)–O(n⁴) scan directly, which is fine for schedules of a few dozen steps.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** of the lost update: T1 reads `stock` (say 5). T2 reads 5, writes 4, commits. T1 writes 4 (computed
from its stale 5). Pattern: A read at 0, B write at 2, B commit at 3, A write at 4 with no re-read between 3 and
4 → `lost update`. No second read by T1, so it is not a non-repeatable read.

Which isolation level prevents what (SQL standard):

| level | dirty read | non-repeatable read | phantom read |
|---|---|---|---|
| READ_UNCOMMITTED | possible | possible | possible |
| READ_COMMITTED | prevented | possible | possible |
| REPEATABLE_READ | prevented | prevented | possible |
| SERIALIZABLE | prevented | prevented | prevented |

```java
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public void reserve(long bookId, int quantity) {
    int stock = repository.readStock(bookId);
    repository.writeStock(bookId, stock - quantity);
}
```
guide.complexity: Time O(n³) in the worst case with these loops; space O(1) beyond the result.
guide.pitfalls: Calling a read after the writer **committed** a dirty read; ignoring that a rollback ends the writer; requiring a second read for the lost update; matching inserts whose key does not start with the scanned prefix.
guide.follow_up: Add *write skew*: two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows based on it.

spring-derived-query.title: Derived queries: from method name to filter
spring-derived-query.description:
Spring Data builds a query from a repository **method name** such as `findByAuthorAndPriceLessThanOrderByTitleAsc`.
Write the translator and run the result against a list of rows.

`run_query(method, args, rows)` — `rows` is a list of dicts, `args` the method arguments in order.

**Grammar**

```
<subject>By<predicate>[OrderBy<ordering>]
```

- Subject: `find` (return matching rows), `count` (return how many), `exists` (return a boolean). `find` may be
  followed by `First` or `Top` and an optional number (`findFirstBy`, `findTop3By`), limiting the rows returned
  after sorting; no number means 1.
- Predicate: conditions joined by `And` / `Or`. Split on `Or` first, then each part on `And`, so `And` binds
  tighter. Only split where the keyword is followed by an upper-case letter. The predicate may be empty
  (`findByOrderByPriceAsc` selects everything).
- Condition: a property name optionally followed by one keyword. The row field is the property with its first
  letter lower-cased (`InStock` → `inStock`).

| keyword | arguments | true when |
|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | 1 | field == arg |
| `Not` | 1 | field != arg |
| `GreaterThan`, `GreaterThanEqual`, `LessThan`, `LessThanEqual` | 1 | field compared with arg |
| `Between` | 2 | low <= field <= high |
| `StartingWith`, `Containing` | 1 | string test |
| `In` | 1 (a list) | field is in the list |
| `IgnoreCase` | 1 | equal ignoring case |
| `IsNull`, `IsNotNull` | 0 | field is / is not `None` |
| `True`, `False` | 0 | field is `True` / `False` |

  A field holding `None` makes every keyword false except `IsNull` (and plain equality/`Not` compare normally).
  Arguments are consumed left to right.
- Ordering: one or more `<Property>Asc` / `<Property>Desc` written one after another; earlier ones are more
  significant. Without an ordering, keep the input order. Sorting is stable.

**Example:** `run_query("findByAuthorAndPriceLessThanOrderByTitleAsc", ["Austen", 9], books)` returns the Austen
books cheaper than 9, by title.
spring-derived-query.starter:
def run_query(method: str, args: list, rows: list):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Spring Data repositories: derived queries and @Query*. Regular expressions, `sorted` with keys.
guide.intuition: The method name is a tiny language. Parse it into a structure — subject, OR-groups of AND-ed conditions, ordering, limit — and only then touch the data. Mixing parsing with filtering is where solutions go wrong.
hints: Peel the name from the outside in: subject and limit, then split off `OrderBy`, then `Or`, then `And`.
For each condition find the keyword by testing suffixes, longest first (`GreaterThanEqual` before `GreaterThan`, `IsNotNull` before `IsNull`).
Sort by the *last* ordering property first; stable sorts then leave the first property dominant.
guide.brute_force: Hard-code the handful of method names you expect. Spring Data exists precisely so nobody has to.
guide.complexity: Parsing is O(length of the name). Filtering is O(rows × conditions); sorting O(k · r log r) for k ordering keys.
guide.pitfalls: Evaluating `And`/`Or` strictly left to right instead of giving `And` precedence; matching `GreaterThan` when the name says `GreaterThanEqual`; consuming an argument for `True`/`IsNull`; applying the limit before sorting; comparing `None` with `<`, which raises in Python.
guide.follow_up: Real names may traverse relations (`findByAuthorCountryCode`). When names grow that long, switch to `@Query`.

spring-page-request.title: Build a Page from a PageRequest
spring-page-request.description:
Repository methods accept a `Pageable` (page number, page size, sort) and return a `Page` that carries one slice
of the data plus enough numbers for a UI to draw "page 2 of 7".

`page(items, number, size, sort)`:

- `items` — list of dicts (the full query result),
- `number` — zero-based page index, `size` — rows per page,
- `sort` — list of `[field, direction]` with direction `"asc"` or `"desc"`; the first entry is the most
  significant; an empty list keeps the given order. Sorting is stable.

If `number < 0` return the string `"Page index must not be less than zero"`. If `size < 1` return
`"Page size must not be less than one"` (check the index first).

Otherwise return a dict with:

`content` (the rows of that page, possibly empty), `number`, `size`, `totalElements`, `totalPages`
(ceiling of total / size, `0` when there are no rows), `numberOfElements` (rows in this page), `first`
(`number == 0`), `last` (there is no later page: `number + 1 >= totalPages`), `hasNext` (`number + 1 < totalPages`).

**Example:** 11 rows, `page(rows, 2, 5, [])` → content has 1 row, `totalPages = 3`, `last = True`, `first = False`.
spring-page-request.starter:
def page(items: list, number: int, size: int, sort: list):
    pass
spring-page-request.solution:
def page(items, number, size, sort):
    if number < 0:
        return "Page index must not be less than zero"
    if size < 1:
        return "Page size must not be less than one"
    ordered = list(items)
    for field, direction in reversed(sort):
        ordered.sort(key=lambda row: row[field], reverse=(direction == "desc"))
    total = len(ordered)
    total_pages = (total + size - 1) // size
    content = ordered[number * size:(number + 1) * size]
    return {
        "content": content,
        "number": number,
        "size": size,
        "totalElements": total,
        "totalPages": total_pages,
        "numberOfElements": len(content),
        "first": number == 0,
        "last": number + 1 >= total_pages,
        "hasNext": number + 1 < total_pages,
    }

guide.prereqs: List slicing and integer division. Lesson: *Spring Data repositories: derived queries and @Query*.
guide.intuition: A page is a slice plus arithmetic. The arithmetic has three classic off-by-one traps: zero-based page numbers, the ceiling division, and the empty result.
hints: Sort a copy first, then slice `[number*size : (number+1)*size]`; Python slices past the end are empty, not errors.
Ceiling division without floats: `(total + size - 1) // size`.
Express `last` and `hasNext` with `number + 1` and `totalPages`; check them against the empty case.
guide.brute_force: Chunk the whole list into pages and index the list of chunks. Correct, but it builds every page to return one, and a page number past the end needs special handling.
guide.approach:
**Dry run:** 11 rows, `number = 2`, `size = 5`. `totalPages = (11 + 4) // 5 = 3`. Slice `[10:15]` → one row.
`first = False`, `last = 3 >= 3 = True`, `hasNext = False`.

Empty table: `totalPages = 0`, so page 0 is both `first` and `last`.

```java
Page<Book> result = bookRepository.findByGenre(
        "scifi", PageRequest.of(2, 5, Sort.by(Sort.Order.asc("genre"), Sort.Order.desc("price"))));

result.getContent();        // the rows
result.getTotalElements();  // needs an extra "select count(*)" query
result.hasNext();
```

A database does this with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10`. Use `Slice` instead of `Page` to skip the count query.
guide.complexity: Time O(k · n log n) for k sort keys (a database would use an index). Space O(n) for the copy.
guide.pitfalls: Treating page numbers as one-based; `total // size + 1` (wrong when total divides evenly and for an empty result); sorting the most significant key last; mutating the caller's list.
guide.follow_up: Deep `OFFSET` pagination gets slow. Sketch keyset pagination (`WHERE id > :lastSeen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`).

tests.expected: Page index must not be less than zero
Page size must not be less than one
Page index must not be less than zero

spring-n-plus-one.title: Count the queries: the N+1 problem and its fixes
spring-n-plus-one.description:
An `Author` entity has a collection of `Book`s. The application runs `authorRepository.findAll()` (one query
returning `n` authors) and then touches `author.getBooks()` for some authors. How many SQL statements run in
total?

`count_queries(n, strategy, accesses, batch_size)`:

- `n` — number of authors returned (indexes `0 .. n-1`),
- `accesses` — list of author indexes whose book collection is read, in order (repeats allowed),
- `strategy` — how the collection is fetched:

| strategy | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `"lazy"` | the first time an author's collection is read, one query loads it; later reads are free |
| `"eager-select"` | right after the first query, one extra query per author runs immediately, whether or not the collection is used |
| `"join-fetch"` | the first query joins the books (`JOIN FETCH` / `@EntityGraph`): no further queries |
| `"subselect"` | the first time **any** collection is read, one query loads the collections of all authors |
| `"batch"` | reading an uninitialised collection runs one query that loads it **together with** the collections of the next uninitialised authors by lowest index, up to `batch_size` collections in total |

`batch_size` is only used by `"batch"`.

Return the total number of queries, including the initial one.

**Example:** `count_queries(100, "lazy", list(range(100)), 0)` → `101` (the "N+1" problem).
With `"batch"` and `batch_size = 25` → `5`.
spring-n-plus-one.starter:
def count_queries(n: int, strategy: str, accesses: list, batch_size: int) -> int:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *JPA basics: entity mapping, relationships and the N+1 problem*.
guide.intuition: Count round trips to the database, not rows. Lazy loading turns a loop over N parents into N extra round trips; every fix works by loading many collections per round trip.
hints: Three strategies have closed-form answers. Only `lazy` and `batch` need simulation.
Keep a boolean per author: is its collection loaded yet?
For `batch`, after loading the requested author, sweep from index 0 marking unloaded authors until the batch is full.
guide.brute_force: Simulating every strategy step by step is fine and is what the solution does for two of them.
guide.complexity: Time O(accesses + n · batches) for the naive batch sweep; O(1) for the closed forms. Space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Counting repeated reads of the same collection; thinking `EAGER` solves N+1 (with a list query it *guarantees* N extra selects); computing batches as `ceil(n / size)` even when few collections are touched.
guide.follow_up: `JOIN FETCH` with pagination loads everything into memory. Why, and what do DTO projections change?

spring-connection-pool.title: Simulate a connection pool with a timeout
spring-connection-pool.description:
Opening a database connection is slow, so applications keep a fixed **pool** of open connections (Spring Boot
uses HikariCP). A request borrows a connection, uses it, and returns it. If all connections are busy the request
waits in a first-come-first-served queue, but only up to a **connection timeout**.

`simulate(pool_size, timeout, requests)`:

- `pool_size` — number of connections (≥ 1), `timeout` — maximum wait in milliseconds (≥ 0),
- `requests` — list of `[arrival, hold]` sorted by arrival time (ties keep list order): the request asks for a
  connection at time `arrival` and, once it has one, keeps it for `hold` milliseconds.

A connection released at time *t* can be handed to a waiting request at the same time *t*. A request gets the
earliest available connection; earlier requests in the list are always served before later ones. If a request
would have to wait **longer than** `timeout` (waiting exactly `timeout` is still fine), it gives up at
`arrival + timeout` without ever holding a connection.

Return, for each request in order, the time it **obtained** its connection, or `-1` if it timed out.

**Example:** `simulate(1, 50, [[0, 100], [10, 10], [60, 10]])` → `[0, -1, 100]`: the second request would wait
90 ms; the third waits 40 ms.
spring-connection-pool.starter:
def simulate(pool_size: int, timeout: int, requests: list) -> list:
    pass
spring-connection-pool.solution:
import heapq


def simulate(pool_size, timeout, requests):
    free_at = [0] * pool_size
    heapq.heapify(free_at)
    result = []
    for arrival, hold in requests:
        start = max(arrival, free_at[0])
        if start - arrival > timeout:
            result.append(-1)
            continue
        heapq.heapreplace(free_at, start + hold)
        result.append(start)
    return result

guide.prereqs: Heaps / priority queues (`heapq`). Lesson: *Configuring the DataSource and connection pools*.
guide.intuition: All that matters about a connection is *when it is next free*. Keep those times in a min-heap; the top is the connection the next request in line will get. Because the queue is first-come-first-served, requests can be decided one by one in input order.
hints: Start with `pool_size` zeros in a heap: every connection is free from time 0.
The start time of a request is `max(arrival, earliest free time)`.
A request that times out must leave the heap untouched: it never held a connection.
guide.brute_force: Advance a clock millisecond by millisecond with an explicit waiting queue. Correct but O(total time × pool), hopeless for long holds.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `pool_size = 1, timeout = 50`: heap `[0]`.
`[0,100]` → start 0, heap `[100]`. `[10,10]` → start would be 100, wait 90 > 50 → `-1`, heap unchanged.
`[60,10]` → start 100, wait 40 → OK, heap `[110]`.

Why input order is safe: an earlier request has an earlier (or equal) deadline and priority in the queue, so
nothing a later request does can change its fate.

```yaml
# src/main/resources/application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bookshop
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10        # pool_size
      connection-timeout: 30000    # timeout in ms (the default)
```

```java
// what a timeout looks like in the log:
// SQLTransientConnectionException: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.
```
guide.complexity: Time O(R log P) for R requests and pool size P. Space O(P).
guide.pitfalls: Occupying a connection for a request that timed out; rejecting immediately instead of waiting; an off-by-one on 'exactly the timeout'; forgetting that a connection freed at *t* is usable at *t*.
guide.follow_up: A slow query holding connections is the usual cause of pool exhaustion. How does `@Transactional` around a remote HTTP call make it worse?

spring-web-scope-lifetime.title: Request, session and application scope lifetimes
spring-web-scope-lifetime.description:
In a web application a bean's scope can follow the HTTP traffic. Count how many instances of each bean the
container creates for a stream of events.

`instances(beans, events)`:

- `beans` — dict `name -> scope`, with scope one of `"singleton"`, `"application"`, `"session"`, `"request"`,
  `"prototype"`.
- `events` — in time order, each either
  - `["request", session_id, [bean names used]]` — one HTTP request belonging to the HTTP session `session_id`;
    the list says which beans the request's code touches, in order, possibly the same bean several times; or
  - `["invalidate", session_id]` — the session ends (logout or timeout). A later request with the same id starts
    a brand-new session.

Creation rules:

| scope | a new instance is created… |
|---|---|
| `singleton` | once, at start-up, even if never used |
| `application` | on first use, then shared by everybody for the life of the app |
| `session` | on first use within each HTTP session |
| `request` | on first use within each HTTP request |
| `prototype` | on every single use |

Return a dict `name -> number of instances created`.

**Example:** beans `{"cart": "session", "requestLog": "request"}`, events
`[["request","s1",["cart","requestLog","requestLog"]], ["request","s1",["cart","requestLog"]]]` →
`{"cart": 1, "requestLog": 2}`.
spring-web-scope-lifetime.starter:
def instances(beans: dict, events: list) -> dict:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Request and session scope* and *Application scope and choosing a scope*. Sets and dicts.
guide.intuition: Each scope is a storage box with a different lifetime. Using a bean means: look in the box that matches its scope; create and store it only if it is not there. The boxes differ only in when they are thrown away.
hints: One set for the application, one set per live session, and a fresh set at the start of every request.
Invalidating a session deletes its set, so the next request with that id starts empty.
Singletons are counted up front; prototypes are counted on every use and stored nowhere.
guide.brute_force: Direct simulation is the solution; the state is three kinds of sets.
guide.complexity: Time O(total uses). Space O(live sessions × session beans).
guide.pitfalls: Counting a request-scoped bean once per use rather than once per request; keeping session state after invalidation; forgetting that the singleton exists even when no request arrives.
guide.follow_up: Session-scoped state breaks when a second server instance is added, unless sessions are stored centrally (Spring Session with Redis) or the app is made stateless.

spring-security-filter-chain.title: Security filter chain: who gets in?
spring-security-filter-chain.description:
Spring Security checks every request against an ordered list of authorization rules. The **first** rule whose
method and path pattern match decides; if none matches, access is denied.

`authorize(rules, request)`:

- `rules` — ordered list of `[method, pattern, access]`. `method` is an HTTP method or `"*"` for any.
- `request` — `{"method", "path", "user"}`; `user` is `None` for an anonymous request, otherwise
  `{"authorities": [...]}`.

**Patterns** are compared segment by segment after splitting on `/`: a literal must be equal, `*` matches exactly
one segment, `**` matches zero or more segments (and may appear anywhere). `/` alone has no segments.

**Access expressions**

| access | allowed when |
|---|---|
| `permitAll` | always |
| `denyAll` | never |
| `authenticated` | there is a user |
| `hasRole:X` | the user has authority `ROLE_X` |
| `hasAnyRole:X,Y` | the user has `ROLE_X` or `ROLE_Y` |
| `hasAuthority:a` | the user has authority `a` exactly |

**Result** `[status, rule_index]`: `200` when allowed. When refused: `401` if the request is anonymous (the
client should log in), `403` if a user is present but not allowed. `rule_index` is the index of the deciding
rule, or `-1` when no rule matched (treated like `denyAll`).

**Example:** rules `[["GET", "/api/books/**", "permitAll"], ["*", "/api/**", "authenticated"]]`; an anonymous
`POST /api/books` → `[401, 1]`.
spring-security-filter-chain.starter:
def authorize(rules: list, request: dict) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Spring Security basics and JWT resource servers*. The request-mapping problem for segment matching.
guide.intuition: Authorization rules are a firewall list: read top to bottom, stop at the first line that matches the request, and let that single line decide. Order therefore matters more than anything else.
hints: Split the work in three functions: does the pattern match, is this access expression satisfied, and the loop.
`**` in the middle needs backtracking: try letting it absorb 0, 1, 2… segments.
